questions.stem: You chair the evaluation panel for a £2.4 million lift replacement across a university's halls of residence. Three bids are in and scoring starts on Monday. On Friday afternoon one of your two technical evaluators mentions in passing that his sister has worked in one bidder's estimating team for six years. He had not thought it mattered, he says, because he has no involvement in her work and did not know she was on this account. What should the project manager do?

options.text: Record the relationship on the procurement file and replace him on the panel with another qualified evaluator.
options.rationale: It puts the interest on the record and removes it from the decision, which is what makes the award survive a challenge. The declaration is as important as the substitution, because an undisclosed interest discovered later is far worse than a disclosed one managed early.

options.text: Keep him on the panel but ask him not to score the bid submitted by his sister's employer.
options.rationale: Partial recusal feels proportionate and is not. Scoring the two competing bids shapes the ranking exactly as much as scoring the connected one, so the interest still reaches the outcome.

options.text: Accept his assurance that he has no involvement in her work and continue as planned.
options.rationale: It treats a conflict as a question of the evaluator's honesty. The test is not whether he would act improperly but what a losing bidder could reasonably infer once the relationship comes out, and it always comes out.

options.text: Ask the bidder to confirm in writing that no information has passed between the evaluator and their estimating team.
options.rationale: It asks the party with the strongest interest in the answer to supply the assurance, and it does nothing about the composition of the panel, which is the only thing actually within your control.

questions.explanation: A conflict of interest is managed for how it will look to the party who loses, not for how much the individual is trusted. The discipline has two halves that are easy to separate and should not be: declare the interest on the record, and remove it from the decision. Interests that are declared and managed almost never become findings; the ones that do are the ones somebody judged too minor to write down.
questions.mindset: Manage an interest for what a losing bidder will reasonably infer, not for how honest you believe the person to be.

questions.stem: Your squad builds practice-management software for a group of veterinary surgeries, and a supplier provides two of the eight developers under a rolling services agreement. The supplier's account manager emails to ask whether she can sit in on the next retrospective. She explains that she wants to understand how her people are getting on and whether the engagement is going well, and that she is happy to observe quietly. How should the project manager respond?

options.text: Decline for the retrospective, and offer her a standing commercial review plus an open invitation to the sprint review.
options.rationale: It protects the one session that depends on candour while giving the supplier two legitimate windows onto progress and the engagement. A supplier with a good view of the work has no reason to want a view of the team's private reflection.

options.text: Agree, on the basis that the supplier's developers are part of the team and openness is healthy.
options.rationale: It conflates being on the team with employing people on the team. Candour drops sharply when someone who influences appraisals and contract renewals is in the room, and the two supplier developers are the ones who lose most.

options.text: Agree, but ask the team beforehand to keep the discussion to process and avoid naming individuals.
options.rationale: Curating a retrospective so it is safe to overhear removes the only thing it exists for. You keep the meeting and lose its function, which is worse than declining.

options.text: Decline, explaining that anything to do with supplier performance is discussed only at contract review.
options.rationale: Right on the retrospective and needlessly closed everywhere else. Shutting the door on the sprint review as well denies the supplier a view of progress that costs nothing to give and builds the trust that makes hard conversations easier later.

questions.explanation: Not every forum on a project is open to everyone with a legitimate interest, and the dividing line is what the forum needs in order to work. Sessions that produce information can take an audience; sessions that depend on people speaking without calculating the consequences cannot. Declining is easier to do well when an alternative is offered in the same breath, because the underlying request is usually reasonable even when the venue is wrong.
questions.mindset: Give a supplier every window onto the work and none onto the team's private reflection.

questions.stem: You issued an invitation to tender for telematics across a county council's winter gritting fleet. Nine days before the deadline, one of five bidders asks a clarification question that exposes a contradiction in your documents: the specification requires position readings every thirty seconds, while the pricing schedule is built on a per-vehicle monthly rate that assumes five-minute polling. The two figures produce very different data costs. Two suppliers have already submitted. What should the project manager do?

options.text: Issue a corrected addendum to every bidder, publish the clarification, and extend the deadline so that submitted bids can be revised.
options.rationale: It restores a common factual basis and gives the bidders who moved early the chance not to be punished for it. The extension is not a courtesy; without it, two bids are priced against a document that no longer exists.

options.text: Answer the question privately to the bidder who raised it and leave the tender documents unchanged.
options.rationale: It rewards the bidder who read most carefully with information the others are pricing without. Private answers are the most common way a properly intentioned tender becomes indefensible.

options.text: Let the tender run and resolve the contradiction with the successful bidder during contract negotiation.
options.rationale: It defers a known defect to the moment competitive pressure ends. Bids priced on two readings of the same requirement cannot be compared, and the negotiation opens with an argument about what was bought.

options.text: Cancel the tender and re-issue it once the specification and pricing schedule have been reworked.
options.rationale: It treats an addendum-sized problem as a fatal one. Cancelling burns every bidder's effort and weeks of programme for a contradiction that a corrected document and a longer deadline resolve.

questions.explanation: Information given to one bidder is information owed to all of them on the same day, and that principle is what makes the clarification process worth running at all. Defects found during a tender are cheap to correct and expensive to carry: the cost of an addendum is a few days, while the cost of an ambiguity that survives to award is paid in disputed scope for the life of the contract. Deadlines exist to serve equal footing, so extending one to preserve it is not a concession.
questions.mindset: Anything one bidder learns from you, every bidder learns from you, on the same day.

questions.stem: A museum wants 400,000 photographic negatives digitised over two years and has asked you to take the work to market. The head of collections has written the requirement, and it reads in full: high-quality digital copies of the negatives, catalogued to a professional standard. Suppliers will price whatever you put in front of them, and four have already expressed interest. Which two actions should the project manager take before the invitation to tender is issued?

options.text: Define measurable acceptance criteria — resolution, colour accuracy, required metadata fields and a tolerated error rate — against a sampled batch.
options.rationale: It converts a word that means something different to every reader into a specification a supplier can price and a museum can reject work against. Sampling makes the criteria enforceable across 400,000 items rather than only in principle.

options.text: Agree with the head of collections how quality will be verified in practice and who signs each batch off.
options.rationale: Criteria without a named verifier and a rhythm for applying them turn into an argument at the end. Settling this before the market sees the pack also forces the requirement owner to commit to what they will actually accept.

options.text: Ask each supplier to propose the quality standard they intend to work to, and score the proposals.
options.rationale: It hands the definition of good to the people being paid to meet it, and it makes the bids incomparable: each is priced against a different product, so the cheapest is simply the one that promised least.

options.text: Keep the phrase professional standard and rely on the supplier's professional obligations to give it meaning.
options.rationale: Undefined quality language does not disappear; it moves the argument to acceptance, which is the point at which the buyer has already paid for most of the work and has least leverage.

options.text: Set a fixed price per negative in the tender so that the bids are directly comparable.
options.rationale: It buys comparability of price without comparability of scope. With quality undefined, a per-item price simply selects the supplier willing to do the least for it.

questions.explanation: The work of a statement of work is to make acceptance decidable before anyone quotes. Quality words carried over from a curator's vocabulary — professional, high-quality, appropriate — feel like requirements and function as blank cheques written in both directions, because the buyer imagines one standard and the seller prices another. The check on any requirement is whether two reasonable people reading it would reject the same batch of work; if they would not, the requirement is a topic rather than a specification.
questions.mindset: Decide what acceptable means before anyone quotes for it, because afterwards it is a negotiation.

questions.stem: Your further education college holds a framework agreement with four IT support suppliers, under which any package above £50,000 must be let by mini-competition among them. The director of estates asks you to place a £120,000 network refresh directly with the supplier who handled last year's cabling. His reasoning is that they know the site, the framework has already tested the market, and a mini-competition would add six weeks to a summer window that is already tight. What should the project manager do?

options.text: Run the mini-competition the framework requires, and make site knowledge one of the evaluation criteria.
options.rationale: It follows the rule and still gives the incumbent's genuine advantage its proper weight, scored rather than assumed. If site knowledge is worth what the director thinks, the incumbent wins on it openly.

options.text: Place the order directly, on the basis that the framework already established that all four suppliers are capable and competitively priced.
options.rationale: It confuses being admitted to a framework with having won this particular call-off. The framework tested capability and rate cards in the abstract; it did not test anyone's price for this network in this building.

options.text: Place the order directly, but ask the other three suppliers for indicative prices first as a benchmark.
options.rationale: It dresses a direct award as competition. Three suppliers spend real effort pricing work they were never going to be given, which is the fastest way to lose their interest in the framework altogether.

options.text: Escalate to the audit committee to ask whether the framework's call-off rules can be waived for programme reasons.
options.rationale: It escalates a rule that is not actually in doubt and invites a governance body to weaken its own controls. Six weeks of inconvenience is not the kind of exception a waiver exists for.

questions.explanation: A framework shortens qualification, not competition: it establishes who may be asked, while the call-off establishes who gets the work and at what price. The pressure to skip the second step almost always arrives as a schedule argument, and it is worth separating the two questions that argument merges — whether the rule applies, which is rarely in doubt, and how to protect the date, which is a planning problem with its own answers. An incumbent's advantage survives being tested; if it does not, it was a preference.
questions.mindset: A framework is a shortcut through qualification, never a shortcut past competition.

questions.stem: Your commercial team is settling terms on three unrelated contracts for a regional insurer in the same month, and each carries an exposure the standard terms leave uncovered. Your finance director has asked which protection to negotiate into each, and has warned that every one of them costs the insurer something in price or goodwill. Match each situation to the protection that answers the exposure it actually creates. One choice is not used.

prompts.text: A twelve-person software house is building your bespoke policy administration system. If the firm fails, you lose access to the source of the system that runs the business.
A civil engineering contractor is rebuilding the head office car park. Latent defects in surfacing of this kind typically appear one or two winters after handover.
A specialist manufacturer is building a single bespoke switchgear unit. If they fail to deliver it, your substation works stop, and that cost dwarfs the £400,000 contract.

options.text: Source code escrow, released on defined insolvency triggers
options.rationale: The exposure is loss of access to something that continues to exist after the supplier does not. Escrow addresses exactly that and nothing else, which is why it is worth negotiating here and pointless on the other two.

options.text: A retention withheld from each payment, released after the defects liability period
options.rationale: The risk is not failure to deliver but failure that only becomes visible later. Retention keeps money in your hands over the window in which the defect appears, which is what makes the contractor answer the telephone in year two.

options.text: A performance bond issued by the supplier's bank
options.rationale: Where non-delivery costs far more than the contract, a remedy limited to the supplier's own resources is no remedy. A bond converts failure into money payable by a third party who is good for it, without waiting for the supplier's balance sheet.

options.text: A parent company guarantee
options.rationale: Not used. A guarantee makes a stronger group entity answerable for a subsidiary's obligations, so it needs a parent worth calling on. A twelve-person software house, a civils contractor and a single-site manufacturer offer nothing behind them for the guarantee to reach.

questions.explanation: Contractual security is chosen by the shape of the exposure and when it bites, not by how reassuring the instrument sounds. Three questions separate them: is the risk that the supplier stops existing, that the defect arrives late, or that non-performance costs a multiple of the contract? Each has an instrument built for it, and each instrument is paid for in price, so buying several where one fits is a real cost. The instrument that protects nothing is the expensive one.
questions.mindset: Choose security for what you would need on the day it goes wrong, not for how much comfort it gives on the day you sign.

questions.stem: An insurer's claims squad includes a supplier team paid a fixed rate for each story point delivered, an arrangement agreed a year ago to reward throughput. Velocity has risen forty per cent over two quarters, but the number of claims journeys actually released has not moved. Looking through the backlog, you find estimates for comparable work have drifted from three points to eight, and the supplier's delivery lead has stopped challenging them in refinement. What should the project manager do?

options.text: Move the supplier's payment onto accepted outcomes or a capacity rate, and re-baseline estimates with the whole team.
options.rationale: It removes the reason to inflate rather than policing the inflation, and re-baselining acknowledges that the existing numbers are unusable. Paying for capacity or for accepted work leaves the estimate free to be an estimate again.

options.text: Cap the points any single story may carry and audit estimates before they enter a sprint.
options.rationale: It polices a corrupted measure instead of removing the corruption. The cap becomes the new target, refinement turns into a negotiation, and you have added permanent overhead to keep a broken mechanism running.

options.text: Raise supplier performance formally, on the basis that inflated estimates are a breach of good faith.
options.rationale: It treats a predictable response to an incentive as misconduct. The contract asked for points and is receiving points; a good-faith argument here is hard to win and poisons a team that has to keep working together.

options.text: Keep the mechanism and compare velocity against the older baseline, discounting for the inflation you have observed.
options.rationale: It invents a correction factor for a number that has stopped measuring anything, and the factor itself will drift. You end up with two fictions instead of one.

questions.explanation: Whatever a contract pays for is what it will receive, and the danger is greatest when the quantity being paid for is also produced by the party being paid. An estimate is a forecast until it becomes a price, at which point it becomes a negotiating position, and no amount of oversight restores it. The response to a perverse incentive is to change what is bought — accepted outcomes, or simply the time of a team — rather than to add controls that assume the incentive can be supervised into behaving.
questions.mindset: Never price a number the supplier also produces.

questions.stem: Your product routes deliveries for a cycle-logistics firm and calls a small vendor's routing engine on every job. Over six weeks their support replies have slowed from hours to days, two named engineers you worked with have left, their status page shows three unexplained outages, and a trade publication reports the company has missed a funding round. Your contract runs another eleven months and the product cannot function without them. What should the project manager do first?

options.text: Establish how long the product could run without them and what switching would cost, and read that against the contract's exit and data export terms.
options.rationale: It answers the question every other option assumes: what your exposure actually is. Knowing your runway, your switching cost and your contractual rights is what turns a rumour into a decision, and it is the one step that improves every subsequent move.

options.text: Raise the concerns with the vendor's chief executive and ask for reassurance about the company's financial position.
options.rationale: It asks for an answer you cannot verify and would not act on, and it signals your concern before you know your own position. A vendor in difficulty has every reason to reassure you and little ability to prove anything.

options.text: Start building an in-house replacement for the routing engine immediately.
options.rationale: It commits substantial capacity on the strength of a signal, before anyone has priced switching or looked at hosted alternatives. Rebuilding is usually the most expensive of the available exits and it is being chosen first rather than last.

options.text: Add vendor failure to the risk register with a high impact score and review it at the monthly risk meeting.
options.rationale: It records the risk at precisely the moment recording stops being useful. Monthly review is the wrong cadence for a dependency showing weekly deterioration, and the register does not tell you what your options cost.

questions.explanation: A supplier's distress converts a commercial relationship into a continuity problem, and the first move is diagnostic rather than remedial: how long you could survive, what leaving would cost, and what the contract already entitles you to. Every negotiating and technical option improves once those three are known, and all of them are harder to establish after a failure than before one. The reason to price an exit early is that the price rises exactly as the need becomes urgent.
questions.mindset: The moment to learn what leaving a supplier costs is while you still have a choice about it.

questions.stem: A £600,000 contract to replace the plant room at a council swimming pool sets liquidated damages at £1,500 for each day completion is late, capped at five per cent of the contract sum. Handover is now forecast forty working days late. The pool is losing roughly £2,300 a day in memberships and lost hire while it stays closed, and the leisure director has asked what the damages clause will actually recover. Work the figures through.

blanks.label: The liquidated damages cap, in £
blanks.rationale: Five per cent of £600,000 is £30,000. The cap limits what the contractor can be made to pay; it says nothing about what the council loses, and the two figures are unrelated by design.

blanks.label: The number of late days the cap covers, to the nearest whole day
blanks.rationale: £30,000 divided by £1,500 a day is twenty days. From day twenty-one onwards, further lateness recovers nothing at all under this clause, and the contractor's financial incentive to finish flattens out.

blanks.label: Who carries the loss arising from days twenty-one to forty
blanks.rationale: Beyond the cap the contractor's liability stops, so about twenty days at roughly £2,300 fall on the council, near £46,000 uncovered. Agreeing a cap is agreeing the point at which the buyer begins to self-insure.

questions.explanation: Liquidated damages are a pre-agreed remedy that spares both sides from proving loss, and the number that matters when negotiating one is not the daily rate but the cap set against the buyer's actual exposure profile. A cap that is exhausted early converts every further day of delay into an unfunded loss and, worse, removes the pressure the clause was supposed to apply. It is also worth remembering what damages do and do not do: they compensate, and no rate of recovery reopens a pool.
questions.mindset: Read a damages cap as the day on which the delay becomes yours.

questions.stem: The analytics platform your squad uses to measure a farm-shop marketplace renews automatically in six weeks at €41,000, up from €31,500, unless notice is given thirty days beforehand. The product owner's view is that the team knows the tool well, migrating mid-quarter would cost sprints, and the increase is irritating but affordable. Nobody has looked at what else is available for three years. What should the project manager do?

options.text: Use the weeks before the notice date to price two alternatives and the real cost of migrating, then negotiate the renewal from that position.
options.rationale: It builds the only leverage a renewal offers, which is a credible alternative, and it does so while the notice window still makes the alternative credible. The work is useful whether you switch or stay.

options.text: Renew at the quoted price and review the market next year when the team has more capacity.
options.rationale: It gives up the leverage without testing it, and next year the same notice date arrives with the same reasoning available. Uplifts compound precisely because each individual one is affordable.

options.text: Serve notice to terminate straight away to force the vendor to improve their offer.
options.rationale: It is brinkmanship without a fallback. If the vendor declines to move, you own an unplanned migration on their timetable rather than yours.

options.text: Ask the vendor to justify the increase and accept it if the explanation is reasonable.
options.rationale: It makes the seller the judge of their own price. Reasonableness is not a benchmark, and a well-argued thirty per cent rise is still a thirty per cent rise.

questions.explanation: A renewal is a purchase, and the notice window is the only period in which the buyer holds anything. Leverage in any purchase comes from a known alternative, so the work is to find out what the alternative costs — including migration, retraining and lost time — before the date on which declining stops being possible. That figure is worth having even when the decision is to stay, because it is the number that makes the next conversation about price a negotiation rather than a request.
questions.mindset: Know what your alternative costs before the notice date, because after it you are not negotiating.

questions.stem: A charity's donor system is supported by a supplier who has just mentioned, during a routine account call, that first-line support moves to their office in another country next month. Support staff can see donor names, addresses, giving histories and, for donors who explained why they gave, health information. Your contract names a single processing location and says nothing about international transfers. Go-live is in three weeks. What should the project manager do?

options.text: Treat the move as a change to the contract and hold it until transfer terms and safeguards are agreed in writing.
options.rationale: Where processing happens is a term the supplier is proposing to change unilaterally, and the buyer's consent is the control. Holding the move keeps the decision where the obligation sits rather than where the convenience does.

options.text: Ask the supplier to confirm that their offshore team is trained in data protection, and record it in the risk register.
options.rationale: It substitutes an assurance for the legal basis that is missing. Training is a sensible thing to want and is not the thing the contract and the law require here, so the gap is documented rather than closed.

options.text: Allow the move but instruct the supplier that offshore staff must not open records containing health information.
options.rationale: It is a control the buyer cannot verify, applied to data the supplier's own system presents on a single screen. Restrictions that depend on someone else's discipline and tooling are not restrictions.

options.text: Escalate to the sponsor to decide whether the go-live date or the data question takes priority.
options.rationale: It frames a legal obligation as a schedule trade-off, which invites the answer that the date matters more. Some questions should not be put to a sponsor as a choice, because posing them that way is itself the error.

questions.explanation: Where and by whom personal data is processed is a contractual term, not an operational detail of the supplier's business, and a supplier's internal reorganisation does not change what they agreed to. Two habits keep this straightforward: read announcements from a supplier against the terms rather than against the relationship, and resist converting an obligation into a priority call. Obligations do not compete with dates; they constrain them, and a date protected by an unlawful transfer was never actually protected.
questions.mindset: Where the data is handled is a term of the contract, not an operational detail of the supplier's business.

questions.stem: Your station accessibility programme runs under a standard form contract with a supplier who is performing adequately overall. Two situations have arisen this month, and your commercial manager wants the right contractual route identified before either is raised with the supplier's account team. Complete each sentence with the response that fits. One choice is not used.

prompts.text: The contract names three key personnel and requires your consent before any of them is replaced. The supplier has quietly swapped two for less experienced staff and progress has slowed. The buyer's first step should be to
A funding decision has removed the need for the final third of the works. The supplier is performing well and is not in breach, but the work is no longer wanted. The buyer should treat this as

options.text: invoke the key personnel clause and require the named individuals, or agreed equivalents, to be restored
options.rationale: The clause exists because the buyer priced the contract on named capability. Using it is a proportionate remedy that puts the specific thing that changed back, and it leaves the wider relationship intact.

options.text: a partial termination for convenience, with the compensation the clause provides
options.rationale: Convenience termination is the paid-for right to stop work you no longer need from a supplier who has done nothing wrong. Paying the stated compensation is what makes it available, not a sign the buyer has conceded something.

options.text: a termination for default, ending the contract at the supplier's cost
options.rationale: Not used. Default termination requires a breach going to the root of the contract. Substituting staff without consent is a breach with its own lesser remedy, and a buyer whose funding has changed has no breach to point at whatsoever.

questions.explanation: A well-drafted contract usually contains a remedy proportionate to the problem, and most commercial damage comes from reaching past it. Two habits separate the situations reliably: ask whether the other party has actually failed to do something they promised, and then ask what the smallest instrument is that restores the position. A buyer's change of mind is not a breach at all, and treating it as one converts a priced entitlement into a dispute the buyer will lose.
questions.mindset: Find the clause that fits the problem before reaching for the one that ends the relationship.

questions.stem: A heritage railway contracted your firm to build a ticketing product on a fixed budget with variable scope: £480,000, twelve two-week iterations, priorities set by them at the start of each one. Nine iterations in, they have reordered priorities four times and roughly two thirds of the original feature list exists. At the steering meeting their commercial director says he expects the whole list by iteration twelve, for the agreed price. What should the project manager do?

options.text: Walk them through the trade decisions iteration by iteration, restate the mechanism they bought, and have them prioritise what the remaining three iterations will hold.
options.rationale: It answers the claim with the record of their own choices and then puts the remaining capacity back in their hands. Doing both matters: the history establishes why the list shrank, and the prioritisation stops the meeting ending in a grievance.

options.text: Absorb the shortfall by adding unpaid capacity across the final three iterations to deliver the full list.
options.rationale: It buys peace by teaching the client that the contract's constraint is negotiable if pressed. The same conversation returns at the next engagement, with a precedent attached.

options.text: Raise change requests covering the features displaced by each reprioritisation.
options.rationale: It misreads the contract entirely. The whole purpose of a variable-scope arrangement is that priorities can move without a change request, and formalising them retrospectively looks like an attempt to bill for their flexibility.

options.text: Escalate to your own sponsor and ask for a ruling on what the contract obliges you to deliver.
options.rationale: It turns a conversation about how their choices spent the budget into a contractual dispute, before showing them the evidence that would probably have settled it in the room.

questions.explanation: A fixed budget with variable scope trades certainty of content for certainty of cost, and it only functions when each trade-off is visible at the moment it is made. The obligation this places on the supplier is continuous rather than contractual: every reprioritisation is a decision to defer something, and if that is not recorded and acknowledged when it happens, the client remembers the original list and nothing else. In this kind of arrangement the running record of what was traded away is a deliverable in its own right.
questions.mindset: Where scope is allowed to move, the record of what moved is what protects both sides.

questions.stem: A supermarket chain's till estate is covered by a five-year managed service, now in year three at £2.9 million a year. Two competitors have since let comparable services at prices around fifteen per cent lower. Your supplier is meeting every service level, the contract has no benchmarking clause and no break before year five, and their account director has begun asking about a two-year extension. Which two actions should the project manager take?

options.text: Open the discussion around the extension the supplier wants, and trade the price of the remaining years against it.
options.rationale: In a contract with no break and no benchmarking, the buyer's only leverage is something the other side wants in future. The extension is that thing, and it is worth more to them now than a price concession costs.

options.text: Write benchmarking and break provisions into the requirement for the successor contract while the lesson is fresh.
options.rationale: The reason this position exists is a drafting decision made three years ago. Capturing the fix immediately is the only way it survives to the next procurement, when the same pressure to keep the paperwork simple will reappear.

options.text: Serve notice of dissatisfaction on price and require the supplier to move to the current market rate.
options.rationale: There is no contractual hook for it. Performance is compliant and the price was agreed, so the supplier's rational answer is a polite refusal, and you have shown your hand for nothing.

options.text: Commission an independent market benchmarking exercise and share the findings with the supplier as evidence.
options.rationale: The exercise is worth doing, but presented with nothing to trade it is information the supplier may simply acknowledge. Evidence changes behaviour only when it is attached to a decision the buyer controls.

options.text: Reduce the range of services taken under the contract to bring the annual spend down.
options.rationale: It cuts service the stores rely on in order to fix a price problem, and unit rates typically worsen at lower volume, so the saving is smaller than it looks.

questions.explanation: Halfway through a long contract, a buyer has exactly two sources of leverage: what was drafted in, and what the supplier wants next. Market movement on its own is not a lever, because a compliant supplier is entitled to the price both sides agreed. That makes long-term price protection a drafting question settled before signature — benchmarking, break points, indexation — and it makes a supplier's ambitions the currency of every mid-term conversation. Noticing what they want is often more useful than proving what you are owed.
questions.mindset: Mid-contract you have the leverage you drafted in and the leverage that they want something; there is no third kind.

questions.stem: A water utility is re-tendering its leak detection service. The incumbent has held it nine years and knows which mains actually fail, where crews really spend their time and what the call-out volumes have been. None of that appears in the tender pack, which quotes volumes from the original 2017 contract. Four new bidders have registered interest and two have asked how the volume figures were derived. What should the project manager do?

options.text: Compile the utility's actual operating data into the tender pack for every bidder, and extend the timetable so bids can reflect it.
options.rationale: The data belongs to the utility, not the incumbent, and publishing it is what turns four registrations into four real bids. The extension matters because information arriving late is only useful if there is time to price it.

options.text: Publish the 2017 volumes as they stand and let bidders make their own risk allowance for any difference.
options.rationale: It turns the competition into a guessing contest that only one party is exempt from. The incumbent, who does not have to guess, wins on a price no one else could safely offer.

options.text: Answer the two clarification questions with the real figures and leave the tender pack unchanged.
options.rationale: The information reaches the bidders who thought to ask, while the pack everybody else prices from stays wrong. It also creates a record of the buyer knowing the published figures were misleading.

options.text: Ask the incumbent to confirm the current volumes and publish their statement to all bidders.
options.rationale: It makes a bidder the source of the data their competitors will price against, in a competition that bidder intends to win. Even handled honestly, the arrangement is impossible to defend afterwards.

questions.explanation: Competition requires a common factual base, and in a re-tender the buyer usually holds the facts that matter while an incumbent holds the experience of them. The operating history of a service the buyer pays for is the buyer's asset, and withholding it is a subsidy to whoever already knows it. Two practical tests apply to any re-tender pack: could a competent outsider price this without guessing, and does anything in it advantage the incumbent for reasons other than genuine performance?
questions.mindset: A re-tender is only a competition if the market can see what the incumbent already knows.

questions.stem: Your squad is six weeks into building a haulage telematics app. The supplier providing three of your eight engineers proposes building the mapping and routing layer on their own proprietary framework, which they estimate will save four to six weeks and which their people already know well. The framework is licensed only to their clients and the source is not available. The product is expected to run for years. What should the project manager do?

options.text: Establish what leaving would cost — rewrite effort, licence terms once the engagement ends, and who owns the resulting code — and decide with those figures on the table.
options.rationale: It puts both sides of the comparison in the same units. The six weeks are already quantified; the only reason the trade looks attractive is that nobody has yet quantified what it commits you to.

options.text: Accept the proposal, since six weeks of delivery now outweighs a migration that may never happen.
options.rationale: It compares a measured benefit against an unmeasured cost and unsurprisingly finds in favour of the measured one. The migration is not hypothetical in a product expected to outlive the engagement.

options.text: Reject it and require an open-source alternative as a matter of principle.
options.rationale: It replaces an assessment with a policy. Some proprietary dependencies are worth the tie, and this one has not been examined in either direction, so the decision is arbitrary even though it looks prudent.

options.text: Accept it, adding a contractual obligation for the supplier to migrate the code to an open framework if the engagement ends.
options.rationale: It places costly work on a departing supplier at the exact moment they have least reason to do it well. The obligation is unpriced and, in practice, close to unenforceable.

questions.explanation: A technical decision that only one supplier can maintain is a commercial commitment wearing a technical disguise, and it is usually taken inside delivery where no procurement process is watching. The way to keep such decisions honest is to price the exit at the moment of choosing: what a rewrite would take, what the licence permits after the relationship ends, and who owns what is produced. Dependencies chosen with those numbers visible are often still the right choice, which is the point.
questions.mindset: Price the exit when you take on the dependency, because that is the last moment the price is low.

questions.stem: The chart plots the four compliant bids for a hospital laundry service, with quality score along the horizontal axis and tendered annual price up the vertical. Your own pre-tender estimate was £1.9 million a year. Award is on the best combination of price and quality, and your finance director is delighted with the range. Select the bid that must be investigated before any award is made.

graphic.title: Four tendered annual prices plotted against evaluated quality score
graphic.caption: Select a bid. Use Tab or the arrow keys to move between the plotted bids, then Enter or Space.

regions.label: Bid A — quality 82, price £2.10m
regions.rationale: Being the most expensive compliant bid is not a defect. Investigating the top of the range treats a quality-and-price award as a price-only one, and penalises a bidder for offering what the specification asked for.

regions.label: Bid B — quality 70, price £1.95m
regions.rationale: This bid sits close to the pre-tender estimate on both axes, which is the pattern a well-understood specification produces. There is nothing here that needs explaining before award.

regions.label: Bid C — quality 76, price £1.05m
regions.rationale: At forty-five per cent below the estimate and far below every other bid, on a quality score that is not low, the price does not follow from anything visible. That pattern usually means a misread specification, an arithmetic error, or an intention to recover the difference through variations later.

regions.label: Bid D — quality 55, price £1.82m
regions.rationale: A low quality score is a scoring outcome, not a doubt about the bid's basis. If a bid this weak on quality should not win, the evaluation weighting handles it; verification is for prices that cannot be explained.

questions.explanation: An abnormally low price is a risk signal rather than a bargain, because the money the bidder has not included has to come from somewhere: failure part-way through, quality below what was specified, or a stream of variation claims once the contract is signed. The correct handling is neither to accept nor to exclude but to ask, in writing, for the basis of the price, and to exclude only where the explanation does not hold. Bids are verified against what the buyer expected to pay, which is why a pre-tender estimate is worth producing.
questions.mindset: A price you cannot explain is a risk you have not yet priced.

questions.stem: The diagram shows the pricing arrangements your commercial framework permits, ordered by who carries the cost risk. You are buying five years of drone survey work across an electricity network. Survey volume is fairly predictable, but flying hours vary with weather and the technology is improving fast enough that unit costs should fall. You want visibility of the supplier's actual costs and you want them motivated to reduce them. Select the arrangement that fits.

graphic.title: Five pricing arrangements ordered from seller-carried to buyer-carried cost risk
graphic.caption: Select an arrangement. Use Tab or the arrow keys to move between the bands, then Enter or Space.

regions.label: Firm fixed price — seller carries the cost risk
regions.rationale: A fixed price gives certainty and hides everything behind it. Over five years of varying flying hours the supplier prices a contingency you cannot see, and if costs fall the saving stays with them, which is the opposite of what you said you wanted.

regions.label: Fixed price with incentive fee
regions.rationale: The incentive is right but it sits on a fixed-price base, so the supplier still carries and therefore still conceals the cost detail. You get motivation without the transparency, and weather variation over five years makes the base price a gamble for both sides.

regions.label: Cost reimbursable with incentive fee
regions.rationale: Reimbursement is what makes actual costs visible, and the incentive fee is what makes the supplier want them to fall. Both of your stated conditions are properties of this arrangement, and predictable volume gives you a target credible enough to incentivise against.

regions.label: Cost reimbursable with fixed fee
regions.rationale: It delivers the transparency and none of the motivation. A fee that does not move gives the supplier no financial reason to pursue the cost reductions the improving technology should produce, so the benefit accrues to nobody.

regions.label: Time and materials
regions.rationale: Time and materials suits short, urgent work too small to be worth specifying. Across five years it rewards hours flown rather than network surveyed, which points the supplier's effort in precisely the wrong direction.

questions.explanation: A pricing arrangement is two decisions at once: who carries the cost risk, and what behaviour the fee rewards. How well the work can be described settles the first, and what the buyer needs from the supplier settles the second, which is why the reimbursable forms differ from one another only in the fee. Cost visibility is a property of reimbursement and cannot be added to a fixed-price arrangement by asking nicely, while motivation is a property of the fee and does not arrive on its own.
questions.mindset: Let how well the work can be described decide who carries the cost risk, and let the behaviour you need decide the fee.

questions.stem: A kiln at a brick works has failed and the plant is losing about £18,000 a day. The control card that failed is made by one manufacturer, and the maintenance manager has already telephoned them: they can ship in four days. Your procurement policy requires three quotations above £25,000, and the card with commissioning comes to £41,000. The operations director tells you to raise the order now and sort the paperwork out afterwards. What should the project manager do?

options.text: Place the order under the policy's single-source route, recording the justification and obtaining the approval that route requires, before the order goes out.
options.rationale: Almost every policy has a route for a market with one supplier, and using it takes hours rather than days. The order still goes today, and it goes with the authority and the record that make it defensible.

options.text: Raise the order immediately and complete the justification once the plant is running again.
options.rationale: Retrospective approval is not approval. It leaves the company's own governance breached and the individual who committed the money personally exposed, for a saving of a few hours.

options.text: Seek three quotations as the policy requires, accepting the additional days that will take.
options.rationale: It applies a rule designed for competitive markets to a market with one supplier. The quotations cannot meaningfully exist, and the delay is paid for at £18,000 a day in lost production.

options.text: Ask the operations director to raise the order himself under his own delegated authority.
options.rationale: It moves the exposure rather than resolving it. The policy is still unmet, and the person now carrying the risk is the one who was most eager to bypass it.

questions.explanation: Urgency changes which rule applies, never whether one does. Competition rules generally include a single-source or emergency route precisely because sole suppliers and plant failures are foreseeable, and the discipline that route demands is contemporaneous: the justification and the approval are written before the commitment, not reconstructed after it. A record made at the time is evidence; the same words written a fortnight later are an explanation, and the difference is exactly what an auditor is looking for.
questions.mindset: Urgency changes which rule applies, never whether one does.

questions.stem: Your engineering firm buys fabricated steelwork from a company that is also one of your largest design clients, worth roughly four times the fabrication contract. The fabricator is eight weeks late on two deliveries and the last batch needed rework on site. Your commercial director suggests keeping the performance conversation informal, through your account contact, so that the design relationship is not damaged. What should the project manager do?

options.text: Administer the contract as written, through the named contract managers on both sides, and leave the account relationship to the people who own it.
options.rationale: Separating the two relationships protects both. The supply issue gets the record and the escalation route it needs, while the account conversation is not contaminated by a dispute the account managers cannot settle anyway.

options.text: Follow the commercial director's steer and raise the delivery problems informally with your usual account contact.
options.rationale: It merges two commercial relationships into one conversation. What the other side hears is a customer complaining, and the contemporaneous record that any later claim depends on is never created.

options.text: Issue a formal notice of default to establish the contractual position beyond doubt.
options.rationale: It reaches for the strongest instrument first over lateness and rework that the contract's ordinary performance provisions are designed to handle, and it risks the larger relationship for no additional remedy.

options.text: Ask your sponsor to raise the delivery problems at the next executive account review with the client.
options.rationale: It puts a supply problem in front of the wrong forum and the wrong people, before it has been worked at the level where the facts live. It also stakes the design account on a matter that had a routine route available.

questions.explanation: When one organisation is both buyer and seller, the discipline is to keep the roles in different rooms and different records. Contract administration is fundamentally a record-making activity: notices, meetings, positions taken at the time. Routing it through an account relationship feels like the diplomatic choice and quietly destroys the evidence base, because nobody minutes a friendly telephone call. Keeping the channels separate also protects the account, since a supply dispute handled at its own level rarely reaches the people who renew the larger contract.
questions.mindset: When one organisation is both your buyer and your seller, keep the two conversations in different rooms.

questions.stem: A credit union has asked a design agency to run an eight-week discovery for a member app before any build is committed. The agency proposes a fixed price for the discovery, with the deliverable described as a validated product direction. Your board wants confidence that eight weeks will produce something it can decide on, whether or not the build then goes ahead. Which two provisions should the project manager insist on?

options.text: Named tangible outputs — research findings, a prioritised backlog and a costed build option — delivered whether or not the credit union proceeds.
options.rationale: It converts a phrase that cannot be accepted or rejected into artefacts that can. The board asked to be able to decide, and these are the things a decision is actually made from.

options.text: Intellectual property in everything produced during discovery vesting in the credit union on payment.
options.rationale: Discovery output is research about the credit union's own members and operations. Without this, the material that makes an alternative builder viable stays with the agency, and the choice at the end is not really a choice.

options.text: A commitment from the agency to deliver the build at the price estimated during discovery.
options.rationale: It demands a firm price for work that has not been defined yet, which is the reason discovery is being run. The agency will either refuse or pad the number, and the padded number then anchors the build.

options.text: A right for the credit union to withhold the discovery fee if it decides not to proceed to build.
options.rationale: It makes payment for completed work conditional on a decision the agency does not control. Either the discovery had value or it did not, and this provision quietly pressures the agency to recommend proceeding.

options.text: A requirement that the same agency team transfers onto the build phase at the same day rates.
options.rationale: Rate protection is worth having but is not what makes a discovery decision-useful, and framing continuity as a requirement pre-selects the builder before the discovery has said anything.

questions.explanation: A discovery contract buys a decision, so the provisions that matter are the ones determining what the buyer keeps when the decision is no. Two failures recur: outputs described in language nobody can accept work against, and intellectual property left where it was created, which turns an exploratory engagement into a commitment to the explorer. Both are cheap to fix before signature and effectively unfixable afterwards, when the agency has the material and the buyer has eight weeks of sunk cost.
questions.mindset: Buy a discovery for what you keep if you walk away from it.

questions.stem: Eleven months after a river wall repair completed, your contractor submits a claim for £220,000, attributing it to ground conditions encountered in the second month of the works. The contract required notice within twenty-eight days of any such event, supported by contemporaneous records, and nothing was notified at the time. Your own site diaries from that period do record unusual water ingress. The contractor's managing director has asked to meet and settle it commercially. What should the project manager do?

options.text: Assess entitlement first — what the contract required, what was notified, and what the records on both sides show — and establish that position before any meeting.
options.rationale: Entitlement determines whether anything is owed, and quantum only matters afterwards. Doing this work before the meeting also means the site diaries are read by you rather than produced as a surprise by them.

options.text: Reject the claim on the ground that notice was not given within the twenty-eight days the contract required.
options.rationale: A defensible opening treated as the entire answer. Your own diaries evidence the event, and a bare time-bar rejection where the buyer plainly knew of the conditions invites a dispute that may not go your way.

options.text: Meet as requested and negotiate a settlement figure, to avoid the cost and delay of a formal dispute.
options.rationale: It negotiates a number before establishing whether anything is owed at all. Every figure discussed in that meeting becomes a floor, and the contractor chose the timing precisely because it invites this.

options.text: Pass the claim to your legal team to handle from this point onward.
options.rationale: It hands over a contract administration task at the stage where the project's own records and technical judgement determine the position. Legal advice is worth having on top of that assessment, not instead of it.

questions.explanation: Claims are decided in two stages, entitlement and then quantum, and mixing them is what turns an administrable claim into a dispute. Notice provisions carry real weight, but they are read alongside what the buyer actually knew at the time, so a party sitting on records of the very event it says it was never told about is in a weaker position than the clause suggests. The general discipline is to work out what is owed before working out what to pay, and to enter any settlement conversation from a position rather than in search of one.
questions.mindset: Work out what is owed before working out what to pay.

questions.stem: A car parts distributor's ordering product is built by six of your staff and a supplier's four-person team in another city. Both work on the same codebase and the same backlog. The supplier's delivery lead proposes his team run their own board and their own two-week cadence, synchronising with yours at the end of each iteration, because the supplier's internal reporting needs a different sprint start date. What should the project manager do?

options.text: Keep one backlog and one cadence for the product, and work out how the supplier's internal reporting can be produced from it.
options.rationale: It holds the thing that must be shared and solves the thing that only looked like a constraint. Reporting periods can almost always be derived from delivery data, whereas two sequencing rhythms on one codebase cannot be reconciled.

options.text: Agree to the separate board and cadence, provided the two are reconciled at each synchronisation point.
options.rationale: It accepts two views of one backlog and pays for it forever. Reconciliation becomes a standing tax, and the synchronisation point turns into where dependencies are discovered rather than where they were avoided.

options.text: Agree, but require the supplier's team to adopt your definition of done and your quality gates.
options.rationale: It fixes the quality question and leaves the sequencing question untouched, which is the one that bites on a shared codebase. Two teams can meet the same standard and still block each other constantly.

options.text: Refuse, and require the supplier to change its internal reporting to match your cadence.
options.rationale: Right on the cadence and wrong on ownership. Dictating how a supplier runs its own management reporting spends goodwill on something you could have solved by extracting the figures you already hold.

questions.explanation: One product with one codebase needs one backlog and one rhythm, because sequencing is the thing that cannot be reconciled after the fact. When a supplier raises a constraint, it is worth separating what is genuinely a constraint of theirs from what is a reporting need dressed as one: reporting can nearly always be generated from shared delivery data, so it should adapt rather than fragment the work. Holding the shared mechanics while flexing everything around them is usually available if you look for it.
questions.mindset: Let a supplier's internal reporting adapt to how the product is built, not the other way round.

questions.stem: A condition survey of a school trust's twelve buildings is estimated at £74,000. Competitive tender is required above £50,000 and takes around ten weeks; below it, a single quotation from an approved supplier is permitted. Your estates lead proposes two orders to the same surveying firm — £39,000 for the primaries and £35,000 for the secondaries — because the survey must be complete before the summer works window. What should the project manager do?

options.text: Treat it as one requirement above the threshold, and take the timing problem to whoever can compress the tender or move the works window.
options.rationale: It keeps the requirement whole and moves the real constraint to the people who can act on it. Tender timetables can often be shortened legitimately, and nobody discovers that while they are busy avoiding the tender.

options.text: Issue the two orders, since each covers a distinct group of buildings with its own deliverable.
options.rationale: The separability is being reverse-engineered from where the threshold sits. The test is whether this would have been bought as one requirement if the rule did not exist, and plainly it would.

options.text: Issue one order for £39,000 now and decide on the remaining buildings after the summer window.
options.rationale: The same avoidance with a delay attached. It also commits the trust to the same surveyor for the rest of the work, since the first half of a survey is not usefully re-competed.

options.text: Ask the finance director to approve a waiver of the tender requirement on grounds of urgency.
options.rationale: Better than splitting because it is at least visible, but urgency created by late planning is rarely a valid waiver ground, and asking establishes a precedent that the next late plan will cite.

questions.explanation: Thresholds apply to requirements rather than to orders, so the question is never how the invoices are arranged but what is genuinely being bought. Splitting is tempting because each half is defensible in isolation and the schedule pressure is real, but a single finding of circumvention is the thing an auditor uses to question every other award the project has made. It is also worth noticing that the constraint being protected is usually somebody else's date, and they have not yet been asked whether it can move.
questions.mindset: If the only reason work divides in two is where the threshold sits, it is one piece of work.

questions.stem: You are contracting a supplier to provide two squads for a distribution centre's automation programme on a capacity basis rather than against a fixed scope. Each squad costs £46,000 a month and works in two-week iterations, and the approved supplier budget is £1.38 million. Your sponsor is uneasy, and wants to know how long the arrangement can run and what he is actually committing the programme to. Work the figures through.

blanks.label: Combined cost of both squads per month, in £
blanks.rationale: Two squads at £46,000 each is £92,000 a month. In a capacity arrangement this is the only rate in the contract, which is what makes the commitment easy to state and easy to under-examine.

blanks.label: Number of whole months the approved budget buys
blanks.rationale: £1,380,000 divided by £92,000 is exactly fifteen months. The budget therefore defines the duration precisely, before anyone has said what the squads will build.

blanks.label: The one thing this arrangement does not fix, in a word
blanks.rationale: Cost and duration are both determined by the rate and the budget, so the variable is what the fifteen months are spent on. That is the whole trade: certainty of spend in exchange for scope that is decided as you go.

questions.explanation: A capacity contract buys a team's time rather than a defined deliverable, so the arithmetic settles cost and duration immediately and leaves content entirely open. That makes prioritisation the control mechanism, and it makes the review point — the moment at which the sponsor can stop, continue or redirect — the most important term in the agreement. A sponsor who understands only the monthly rate has understood the commitment and not the risk, which is that fifteen months of capacity can be spent on the wrong things just as easily as the right ones.
questions.mindset: When you buy capacity you buy time, so the thing to govern is what that time gets spent on.

questions.stem: Your pet insurance product is built with a supplier team. Reviewing the last three iterations you find they have shipped a claims photo uploader, a referral scheme and two administrative screens that were never on the backlog. The supplier's lead is proud of them: they were built in slack time at no extra charge, and the operations team is already using one. Two carry no automated tests and none has been through your privacy review. What should the project manager do?

options.text: Bring the delivered work into the backlog as items to be assessed, tested and then accepted or removed, and agree that nothing reaches the product outside it.
options.rationale: It deals with the code that is already live and closes the route that let it get there, without treating a well-intentioned act as misconduct. Assessment allows the genuinely useful feature to stay, on the same terms as everything else.

options.text: Thank the supplier and accept all four features, since they cost nothing and one is already valued by operations.
options.rationale: It prices only the build. Unrequested software carries support, security exposure and permanence, and those costs land on the buyer for years after the slack time that produced it.

options.text: Require the supplier to remove all four features immediately.
options.rationale: It removes something already in operational use without assessing whether it should be, and it punishes initiative rather than redirecting it. The next useful observation from that team will not be made.

options.text: Raise it formally as a breach for delivering work outside the agreed scope.
options.rationale: It reaches for the contract over an act of goodwill and, more importantly, does nothing at all about untested code that is already running in a regulated product.

questions.explanation: Free work is not free: everything that enters a product carries lifetime cost in support, security and constraint on future change, and that cost is borne by the buyer regardless of who wrote it. The control is a single route in — one backlog, one set of gates — applied without exception, because exceptions are always made for the generous cases. Handling this well means separating the behaviour, which deserves redirection rather than sanction, from the artefacts, which need assessing like anything else.
questions.mindset: Nothing enters the product without passing the same gate, however generously it arrived.

questions.stem: You are running the evaluation of tenders for a hospital trust's catering contract, and three problems have surfaced in the same week. The invitation to tender set out the evaluation method, the mandatory requirements and the treatment of incomplete submissions, and two of the bidders are known to be litigious. Match each problem to the response that fits it. One choice is not used.

prompts.text: Two evaluators have scored the same quality response four points apart, and each can explain their reasoning from the evidence in the bid.
A bidder has omitted the signed declaration that the tender documents listed as mandatory, but has answered every question in full.
A submission is complete and well argued but proposes a staffing model below the minimum on-site hours stated as a mandatory requirement.

options.text: Hold a moderation session where the panel discusses the evidence and agrees a consensus score
options.rationale: Divergence between competent evaluators is normal and is information about how the evidence reads. Moderation resolves it by argument from the bid, which is why consensus scoring is defensible in a way that averaging two numbers is not.

options.text: Apply the rule the tender documents stated for incomplete submissions, whatever it says, to this and every bidder alike
options.rationale: The published rule already decided this, and its value comes entirely from being applied uniformly. Deciding afresh now, on the merits of a good bid, is what turns a documented process into a discretionary one.

options.text: Exclude the bid, recording the mandatory requirement it fails to meet
options.rationale: A mandatory requirement that a strong bid can miss was never mandatory. Recording the specific failure is what makes the exclusion explicable at debrief and survivable if challenged.

options.text: Abandon the evaluation and re-run the tender with clearer documents
options.rationale: Not used. Re-tendering answers a process that cannot produce a defensible award at all. Three ordinary evaluation problems, each with a stated rule available, do not amount to that, and re-running would waste every bidder's effort.

questions.explanation: An evaluation is defensible when it does what the published documents said it would do, particularly on the occasions when that costs the buyer a bid it liked. Three habits carry most of the weight: resolve scoring differences by discussing evidence rather than splitting the difference, apply stated rules uniformly rather than case by case, and treat mandatory as a word that means something. The discipline is tested only when following the rules produces an unwelcome outcome, which is precisely when abandoning them is least defensible.
questions.mindset: Decide by the rules you published, especially when applying them costs you a bid you liked.

questions.stem: A wind farm access road contract is finished: the road is in use, the contractor has demobilised and the final invoice has arrived alongside a request to release the retention. Your site team is entirely satisfied with the work. The contract also required as-built drawings, a materials test certificate pack, and a twelve-month defects liability period that has not yet begun to run. Which two actions should the project manager take before final payment is released?

options.text: Verify that every deliverable the contract required has actually been received, including the as-built drawings and the certificate pack.
options.rationale: Documentary obligations are invisible on site and are the ones most often missed, because the physical work looks complete. Final payment is the last moment at which their absence is a problem for the contractor rather than for you.

options.text: Confirm in writing what remains open on both sides — outstanding claims, the defects liability period and the retention arrangements.
options.rationale: Closure means both parties agree what is finished and what continues. Writing it down now prevents a dispute in month eleven about whether a defect falls inside a period nobody documented the start of.

options.text: Release the payment on the strength of the site team's satisfaction with the completed road.
options.rationale: Satisfaction with the visible product is not verification against the contract. The road being good tells you nothing about whether the test certificates exist, and after payment they are very hard to obtain.

options.text: Withhold the final payment until the twelve-month defects liability period has expired.
options.rationale: It confuses retention with payment. The retention mechanism exists precisely so the balance can be settled now while a defined sum remains held, and withholding everything is a breach of the payment terms.

options.text: Ask the contractor to confirm in writing that it has no further claims, and treat that confirmation as closing the contract.
options.rationale: A waiver is worth having but discharges only their side. It does nothing about the buyer's own verification, so undelivered drawings stay undelivered and unnoticed.

questions.explanation: Closing a contract is an act of verification against what was agreed, not against the impression the finished work makes. The obligations most often left unfulfilled are documentary — drawings, certificates, manuals, data — because they are not visible on site and nobody misses them until the asset needs maintaining years later. Final payment is the last leverage the buyer will ever hold on that contract, so the discipline is to spend it on checking rather than on goodwill, and to write down what continues after it.
questions.mindset: Final payment is the last leverage you will ever have; spend it on checking, not on goodwill.

questions.stem: The independent laboratory validating your medical device software has been bought by a large group. Their commercial team has sent through a novation agreement transferring your two-year contract to a different legal entity, and asks you to sign this week so that invoicing is not interrupted. The named test engineers, they say, are unaffected. Eight months remain and your contract requires your consent to any assignment. What should the project manager do?

options.text: Treat consent as a decision to be taken — examine what the new entity brings in capability, accreditation and financial standing, and what the agreement alters in the terms.
options.rationale: A consent right is worth exactly what you do with it. The two questions that matter are who you will be relying on afterwards and what else has changed in a document you did not draft.

options.text: Sign it, since the engineers doing the work and the price you pay are both unchanged.
options.rationale: It reads a contract as a relationship with individuals. Obligations, accreditations, insurances and covenant strength attach to the legal entity being substituted, and that is the thing actually changing.

options.text: Refuse consent and re-tender the remaining eight months of validation work.
options.rationale: It treats a routine corporate event as grounds to abandon a working arrangement, and revalidating a medical device's test provider mid-programme carries real cost and regulatory delay.

options.text: Sign, subject to a side letter naming the current test engineers as key personnel.
options.rationale: It attends to the smallest risk in the transaction while accepting the substitution of the counterparty unexamined. Named engineers are little comfort if the new entity's accreditation differs.

questions.explanation: A novation substitutes the party you are relying on, so the diligence belongs on the entity rather than on the people or the price. Consent rights exist to create exactly this pause, and the pressure to sign quickly is nearly always the other side's administrative convenience rather than a real deadline. It is also worth reading what else the agreement changes, since a novation drafted by the acquirer is an opportunity to adjust terms that the buyer would notice if they were proposed on their own.
questions.mindset: When a contract is passed to a different company, ask what you are now relying on, not who is still doing the work.

questions.stem: A payments squad includes four supplier engineers. Over two iterations, three stories they marked as done have returned from your testers with defects. Reading the supplier's own delivery handbook, you find their definition of done ends at code review, with automated tests treated as a separate later activity billed as test engineering. Your team's definition of done includes tests. The contract mentions neither. What should the project manager do?

options.text: Agree a single definition of done for the product with both sides, and record it as the acceptance standard for the supplier's work.
options.rationale: It settles the ambiguity for the future and makes the standard contractual rather than cultural. Agreeing it jointly also surfaces the cost question honestly, instead of leaving it to be discovered story by story.

options.text: Ask the supplier to adopt your definition of done from the next iteration onwards.
options.rationale: The right destination reached the wrong way. Imposing a standard on work already priced against a different one invites a change request and a reasonable complaint that the goalposts moved.

options.text: Have your own engineers write the missing tests for the supplier's stories.
options.rationale: It absorbs the supplier's cost into your team's capacity and makes the gap permanent by making it painless. The supplier never learns that their output is incomplete for this product.

options.text: Reject the affected stories and withhold payment for the two iterations concerned.
options.rationale: It penalises a supplier for meeting a standard nobody told them differed from yours. The ambiguity was the buyer's to notice, and this response spends trust on a position that is hard to sustain.

questions.explanation: Done is a contractual term whether or not anybody wrote it down, because it determines what is being paid for. Where two organisations build one product, an unstated difference between their standards surfaces as defects at the boundary, and the defects look like a quality problem when they are actually a definitional one. The fix is a single agreed standard recorded as the basis of acceptance, negotiated rather than imposed, because whichever definition wins will change what the work costs.
questions.mindset: If two organisations build one product, done has to mean one thing.

questions.stem: A five-year contract supplies de-icing salt to twelve depots, with prices adjusted each year by a published mineral extraction index. In year three the index has risen four per cent while the supplier's fuel and haulage costs have risen far more, and they say they are now losing money on every load. They have asked for a mid-term uplift outside the mechanism. Their performance has been faultless, and no alternative supplier could cover twelve depots before winter. What should the project manager do?

options.text: Establish what the contract permits, then what continuity is actually worth to the authority, and treat any relief as a negotiated variation with something obtained in return.
options.rationale: It refuses the false choice between refusing and conceding. Pricing continuity turns the supplier's request into a commercial decision, and taking something back — term, volume commitment, service levels — keeps the mechanism meaning something.

options.text: Decline the request, on the basis that both parties agreed an index precisely so that neither would reopen price.
options.rationale: Contractually clean and operationally reckless. The position is only strong if a supplier who stops delivering is an acceptable outcome, and with winter approaching and no alternative in place it plainly is not.

options.text: Agree the uplift the supplier has requested, given their record and the risk to winter operations.
options.rationale: It pays a figure the counterparty chose, without testing it and without obtaining anything for it. It also establishes that requests outside the mechanism succeed, which guarantees more of them.

options.text: Agree an uplift on condition that the index is replaced by an open-book cost recovery mechanism for the remaining two years.
options.rationale: It sounds principled and hands the buyer's cost risk over on the strength of one bad year. Open-book recovery removes the supplier's incentive to control the very costs that caused the problem.

questions.explanation: An index allocates a risk both parties accepted, and it does its job most of the time by making price movement automatic and unarguable. When it bites hard enough to threaten the supplier's viability, the useful question stops being what the contract entitles you to and becomes what continuity is worth against the alternatives, because a supplier who cannot afford to keep delivering is the buyer's problem too. Relief of that kind is bought rather than granted, and it goes through the contract's own variation route so that the reasoning survives audit.
questions.mindset: A supplier who cannot afford to keep delivering is your problem too, but relief is something you buy, not something you grant.

questions.stem: Your squad's observability tool costs £24,000 a year. The vendor's quarter ends on Friday and their representative has offered a three-year deal at £19,500 a year if you commit before then. Renewing annually instead, you expect the list price to rise by roughly eight per cent each year. Your product's future beyond about eighteen months is genuinely unsettled. Work the comparison through before the deadline.

blanks.label: Total cost of the three-year commitment, in £
blanks.rationale: Three years at £19,500 is £58,500, fixed on signature. This is the only figure in the comparison that is certain, which is part of why it feels like the safer number.

blanks.label: Total of three annual renewals at £24,000 rising eight per cent each year, in £ to the nearest hundred
blanks.rationale: £24,000 plus £25,920 plus £27,994 is about £77,914, so roughly £77,900. The three-year deal looks around £19,400 cheaper, but only if you actually use all three years.
