blanks.label: What the three-year commitment costs you that the annual route does not, in a word
blanks.rationale: You are buying a discount by selling the right to stop, and your product's life beyond eighteen months is unsettled. If it is retired in year two, the cheaper deal costs £19,500 for a tool nobody uses.

blanks.label: Roughly how many years of use make the three-year deal worth it, to the nearest year
blanks.rationale: Two years of the annual route costs about £49,900 against £58,500 committed, so the deal only pays back if all three years are used. A commitment that needs its full term to break even is a bet on the product outliving the contract.

questions.explanation: A multi-year discount is the price a vendor pays for removing your option to leave, so the comparison is incomplete until that option is valued. The test is not whether the discounted total is lower but how likely you are to want the later years, and a deal that only breaks even at full term is a bet rather than a saving. A quarter-end deadline is the seller's calendar and rarely the buyer's, and treating it as a constraint is how commitments get made without the arithmetic being done.
questions.mindset: Price the option you are giving up before you price the discount you are being offered.

questions.stem: A hospital pharmacy robot programme is being delivered under a signed contract with a defined statement of work. Three requests have arrived in the same fortnight, and your commercial lead wants each one routed correctly before anybody discusses money with the supplier's account team. Match each request to the route that fits it. One choice is not used.

prompts.text: The trust needs the second dispensing unit commissioned three months earlier than the programme shows, for exactly the scope of work already contracted.
The supplier proposes assembling the conveyor in a different sequence, reaching the same specified outcome at lower cost to itself, with no change to price, dates or performance.
The trust now wants the robot to feed a chemotherapy compounding unit that appears nowhere in the statement of work and requires a different regulatory approval.

options.text: A priced variation under the contract's change provisions
options.rationale: The obligation itself is changing: the same scope against a different date is a different commitment, and acceleration has a cost the supplier is entitled to recover. This is the situation change provisions exist for.

options.text: No contractual change; confirm it in writing as a method decision within the existing terms
options.rationale: Nothing the contract obliges either party to do has altered. How a supplier chooses to perform is generally theirs, so the buyer's interest is a written record that the specified outcome still stands, not a change request.

options.text: A separate procurement, evaluated on its own merits
options.rationale: The requirement itself is new, materially different in kind, and carries its own regulatory route. Absorbing it as a variation would expand the contract well beyond what was competed for, which is where challenges come from.

options.text: Termination of the contract and re-letting of the whole scope
options.rationale: Not used. Termination answers a contract that can no longer deliver what it was let for. Three routine requests during normal delivery, each with a proportionate route available, are nothing like that.

questions.explanation: Routing a request correctly depends on identifying what is actually changing: the obligation, the method, or the requirement. An obligation changing is a variation; a method changing is usually the supplier's business and needs only a record; a new requirement of a different kind is a new procurement, however convenient it would be to add it to a contract already in place. Most disputes about change begin as misroutings, because the cost conversation starts before anyone has settled which of the three is in front of them.
questions.mindset: Before asking what a change costs, ask whether what is changing is the obligation, the method or the requirement.

questions.stem: A supplier squad builds and supports a logistics client's driver app under a services agreement with acceptance criteria agreed for each feature before it is built. Two questions of cost have arisen this iteration, and your commercial lead wants the principle settled before either is raised with the supplier's account team. Complete each sentence with the response that fits. One choice is not used.

prompts.text: A released feature fails against the acceptance criteria that were agreed before it was built, and must be reworked. The cost of that rework should be
The client asks for a feature it accepted two months ago to be reworked, because the depot operation has changed since. The cost of that rework should be

options.text: borne by the supplier, at no charge to the client
options.rationale: Work that does not meet the criteria agreed at the time was never delivered, so putting it right completes the original obligation. Charging for it would let the supplier be paid twice for one feature.

options.text: borne by the client, as new work taken into the backlog
options.rationale: The feature met its criteria and was accepted; what has changed is the client's operation. That is a new requirement, and treating it as a defect would make the supplier insure the client against its own business changes.

options.text: shared between the parties under a pain and gain formula
options.rationale: Not used. Sharing formulas apply where both parties agreed a target and both influence the outcome. Neither situation here is jointly caused: one is work that missed its standard, the other is a requirement that did not exist before.

questions.explanation: Almost every argument about who pays for rework is settled by asking what standard applied when the work was agreed, and whether the work met it. Failure against criteria set beforehand is incomplete delivery; a change of mind afterwards is new work, however reasonable the reason. Keeping those two apart protects both sides, because a supplier asked to absorb the client's changing operation will price that risk into everything else, and a client charged for the supplier's own misses stops trusting acceptance at all.
questions.mindset: Ask what standard applied when the work was agreed, and the question of who pays usually answers itself.

questions.stem: A town centre regeneration programme buys from around forty small suppliers alongside two main contractors. Your finance shared service pays sixty days from invoice receipt and in practice averages seventy-eight. Three suppliers have stopped accepting new orders from you, a scaffolding firm has told your site manager it cannot fund the next phase, and your two best joiners have moved to another client. Which two actions should the project manager take?

options.text: Establish where the delay actually occurs — approval, goods receipting or the payment run — and fix the step adding the extra eighteen days.
options.rationale: Seventy-eight days against a sixty-day term is a process defect rather than a policy, and it usually sits in one identifiable step. Fixing it costs nothing in policy terms and removes the cause rather than its symptoms.

options.text: Put the supply chain's financial exposure on the programme risk register with the specific suppliers named, and take it to the sponsor as a delivery risk rather than a finance matter.
options.rationale: Framing matters here: as a finance issue it competes with working capital policy and loses, while as a delivery risk it belongs to the sponsor who owns the date. Naming suppliers makes the exposure concrete rather than general.

options.text: Offer the affected suppliers earlier payment in exchange for a discount on their invoices.
options.rationale: It charges struggling suppliers for money they are already owed, and dresses the buyer's own payment failure as a commercial opportunity. Word of it travels through a local supply chain quickly.

options.text: Instruct the two main contractors to pay their subcontractors more promptly.
options.rationale: It passes an obligation down a chain you are late paying at the top of. The cash has to come from somewhere, and a contractor funding your delay will price it back into the next package.

options.text: Re-tender the packages held by the suppliers who have stopped accepting orders.
options.rationale: It replaces suppliers who are behaving rationally, at new-entrant prices and with new mobilisation, while leaving the condition that drove them away entirely intact.

questions.explanation: A supply chain's cash health is a delivery risk that happens to be measured in money, and it shows up on the programme as attrition, refused orders and rising prices long before anyone in finance notices anything wrong. Small suppliers cannot absorb what large ones can, so terms that look standard in a payment policy are structurally different in effect at the bottom of the chain. The practical move is usually diagnostic — where the days are actually going — because the gap between the agreed term and the real one is where most of the damage lives.
questions.mindset: Treat your supply chain's cash flow as part of your schedule, because that is where it eventually appears.

questions.stem: You are drafting terms for a two-year development engagement on a local authority's parking app. Your legal team has included a clause letting the authority end the contract at the close of any release, paying for completed work plus a stated exit fee. The supplier objects: their business model needs two years to justify mobilising a team, and they say the clause signals a lack of commitment. What should the project manager do?

options.text: Keep the option, price the exit fee so it genuinely covers mobilisation, and explain what the clause also gives the supplier.
options.rationale: It holds the protection and removes the supplier's real objection, which is unrecovered mobilisation cost rather than the principle. Explaining the mutual benefit turns a clause that reads as distrust into one that reads as a shared discipline.

options.text: Remove the clause to secure the supplier's commitment, relying on the relationship if things go wrong.
options.rationale: It trades the buyer's only structural protection for enthusiasm. The circumstances in which the clause is needed are exactly those in which the relationship has already stopped working.

options.text: Keep the clause as drafted and tell the supplier it is not open to negotiation.
options.rationale: It wins the point and wastes the conversation. The supplier starts the engagement believing the buyer is looking for an exit, and the exit fee is left at a figure that may not cover what it should.

options.text: Replace it with a single break point at twelve months.
options.rationale: It reduces many decision points to one that falls wherever the calendar says, rather than wherever the evidence appears. That is the opposite of what incremental delivery is meant to give the buyer.

questions.explanation: In incremental delivery the buyer's main protection is not a specification but the ability to stop, and that ability is only real if exercising it is priced and predictable. An exit fee is what makes the option acceptable to a supplier who must mobilise, so haggling it down often destroys the clause more effectively than deleting it. Worth saying out loud in the negotiation: a break clause also frees the supplier from being held in work that has stopped delivering value, which is where relationships are usually damaged beyond repair.
questions.mindset: The option to stop is worth paying for, and worth explaining to the person you are asking to accept it.

questions.stem: Six weeks after launch, the vendor whose components underpin your credit scoring product asks to publish a case study naming your organisation, quoting your engineering lead and describing the architecture. Their account manager mentions that a signed case study would help her make the argument for the discount you asked about at renewal. Your product is regulated and your firm has a communications policy. What should the project manager do?

options.text: Route it to the people who own the decision — communications, and whoever owns the security position on describing the architecture — and keep it out of the renewal discussion.
options.rationale: It puts a disclosure decision in front of the functions that make them routinely, and separates it from a price negotiation where it does not belong. Both halves matter: the referral alone is not enough if the trade stays attached.

options.text: Agree, since the publicity is harmless and the discount is worth having.
options.rationale: It trades something that is not the project manager's to trade, and prices the firm's name and its architecture at the size of a software discount.

options.text: Agree in principle, subject to approving the final text before publication.
options.rationale: Approval rights are necessary and not sufficient. Whether a regulated system's architecture should be described publicly at all has still not been asked of anyone qualified to answer it.

options.text: Decline outright, to avoid disclosing anything about the product.
options.rationale: It refuses without consulting the functions that handle such requests routinely, and gives up an ordinary marketing exchange on the project manager's own unexamined caution.

questions.explanation: Some things a supplier asks for belong to the organisation rather than to the project: its name, its reputation, and information about how its regulated systems are built. Recognising a request of that kind is most of the work, and the tell is usually that saying yes would commit something the project manager could not create or replace. The second discipline is keeping such decisions out of a commercial negotiation, because a benefit attached to the request quietly turns a question of judgement into a question of price.
questions.mindset: Notice when a supplier is asking you to spend something that was never yours to spend.

questions.stem: A whistleblower email tells you that the labour agency supplying groundworkers to your modular school building programme is holding workers' identity documents and deducting large sums from their pay for accommodation. The agency sits two tiers below your main contractor. Your contract gives you supply chain audit rights exercisable on fourteen days' notice. Using them will delay a concrete pour that protects a fixed academic year handover. What should the project manager do?

options.text: Act on the allegation now under the audit rights and your organisation's own reporting obligations, and treat the handover date as the thing that moves.
options.rationale: The audit right exists for exactly this and only helps if it is used while the situation is live. Deciding at the outset that the date is what gives way prevents the schedule quietly reshaping the investigation.

options.text: Complete the concrete pour, then exercise the audit rights the following week.
options.rationale: It sequences a possible criminal harm behind a construction milestone. The week saved is trivial against an exposure not measured in weeks, and the delay is precisely what a fourteen-day notice period already gives the agency.

options.text: Ask the main contractor to investigate their subcontractor's agency and report back to you.
options.rationale: It asks the tier with the strongest commercial reason for the answer to be nothing, and puts the chain on notice before any records have been seen. It is also the option that most resembles doing something while doing very little.

options.text: Refer the email to your legal team and pause until advice comes back.
options.rationale: Advice is needed and a pause is not neutral. Workers remain in the situation, and records that fourteen days' notice already threatens are less likely to survive a longer wait.

questions.explanation: Obligations on labour standards run through the whole supply chain, not just to the party you contracted with, and audit rights are negotiated precisely so that a buyer can look past the tier it can see. Allegations of this kind do not queue behind delivery milestones: the harm is continuing, the evidence is perishable, and a buyer who investigated only after the pour will be judged on that sequence. It is also worth noticing that the tier closest to the problem is the tier least able to investigate it impartially.
questions.mindset: Some obligations in a supply chain do not queue behind the programme; they interrupt it.

questions.stem: You invited tenders for the conservation of a county archive's parchment collection. Six suppliers took the documents and one submitted. That bid is compliant and priced eleven per cent above your estimate. Debrief calls reveal that three firms could not meet a requirement for the work to be done in your building, and two said the eight-week turnaround was impossible at that volume. Your sponsor wants to award and move on. Which two actions should the project manager take?

options.text: Test whether the on-site requirement and the eight-week turnaround are genuine constraints or preferences carried over from the previous contract.
options.rationale: Five suppliers named the same two requirements, which makes them the most likely cause of the empty field. Requirements inherited without re-examination are where competition usually goes to die.

options.text: Establish value for money by other means — a cost breakdown, published rates, comparable recent awards — since competition has not established it.
options.rationale: Where the market has not tested the price, the buyer must, and a single bidder knows perfectly well that it is unopposed. This is also the evidence any subsequent audit of the award will look for.

options.text: Award to the only compliant bidder, since the process was properly run and produced a compliant bid.
options.rationale: A valid process is not evidence of a competitive price. Compliance says the bid met the rules; it says nothing about whether the number was disciplined by anyone.

options.text: Re-tender immediately using the same documents to attract wider interest.
options.rationale: It re-runs a competition whose documents are the reason nobody bid, and spends another eight weeks proving the same point. Re-tendering is only useful once something has changed.

options.text: Approach the three firms that could not meet the on-site requirement and invite them to bid outside the process.
options.rationale: It tries to rescue competition by abandoning the rules the one compliant bidder followed, which makes any resulting award indefensible and probably challengeable.

questions.explanation: A single response is information about the specification rather than about the market, and the debrief is where that information is found. Requirements carried over from a previous contract are the usual culprits, because nobody re-tests them and each one silently disqualifies a section of the market. Where competition has failed to discipline the price, the obligation to establish value for money does not disappear; it moves to the buyer, who must build the evidence that a competition would otherwise have produced.
questions.mindset: One bid tells you more about your own requirements than it does about your suppliers.

questions.stem: A developer on your fintech squad has built a reconciliation feature on an open source library and it works well. In code review another engineer notices the library carries a strong copyleft licence, which requires anything distributed with it to be released under the same terms. Your product is licensed to banks and installed on their own infrastructure. The feature is in Thursday's release. What should the project manager do?

options.text: Hold the feature out of Thursday's release and have the licence assessed by whoever owns software licensing in your organisation.
options.rationale: It stops the event that would create the exposure and puts the question to the people qualified to answer it, at a cost of one release. Nothing is decided yet, which is appropriate given nobody has established what the licence actually requires here.

options.text: Ship it as planned, since the library is free to use and the team has done nothing wrong.
options.rationale: It confuses free of charge with free of obligation. An open source licence is a contract, and this one attaches conditions to distribution of a product your firm sells.

options.text: Ship it and remove the library in a later iteration if the licence proves to be a problem.
options.rationale: The obligation attaches on distribution, so the release is the event that creates the exposure. Removing the library afterwards does not undo what shipping it may already have required of you.

options.text: Ask the developer to rewrite the feature without the library before Thursday.
options.rationale: It acts before knowing whether there is a problem, spending the team's week on a rewrite that an assessment might well show to be unnecessary.

questions.explanation: Choosing a dependency is a procurement decision taken at a keyboard, without a contract review or an approval, and open source licences are the case where the terms most often go unread because nothing is paid. The critical fact about copyleft terms is when the obligation is triggered: use inside an organisation is usually unremarkable, while distributing a product is the act that engages the conditions. That makes the release, not the commit, the point of no return, and it makes holding a release the cheapest available response.
questions.mindset: Free to download is not free of obligations, and the obligations arrive when you ship.
